chunks: Ali, from his father, from Abdullah ibn al-Mughira, from Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who said:

Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no word lighter upon the tongue than it, nor more eloquent than 'Subhanallah' (Glory be to Allah).' I said: 'Will it suffice me during the Ruku' and Sujood if I say in place of the Tasbih: 'La ilaha illallah' (There is no god but Allah), 'Alhamdulillah' (Praise be to Allah), and 'Allahu Akbar' (Allah is the Greatest)?' He said: 'Yes, all of that is the Dhikr of Allah.'

He said: I said: 'We know Alhamdulillah and La ilaha illallah, so what is the interpretation of Subhanallah?' He said: 'It is a sense of respect (Anafah) for Allah. Do you not see that when a man is astounded by something, he says 'Subhanallah'?'.

key_terms.أَنَفَةٌ: A sense of respect, awe, or being astounded.
key_terms.سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ: Glory be to Allah; identified as the most eloquent and lightest phrase for glorification.

ai.seo_question: What is the specific meaning and significance of saying 'Subhanallah' during prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) elevates 'Subhanallah' as the most eloquent and effortless dhikr, clarifying that while other phrases suffice for ritual validity, this specific phrase uniquely conveys divine transcendence and awe. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on the qualitative depth of dhikr, where 'Subhanallah' reflects the believer's recognition of God's purity from imperfection, a concept deeply rooted in the theological understanding of Tawhid.

en.hubeali: Ali, from his father, from Abdullah Bin Al Mugheira, from Hisham Bin Al Hakam who said,

‘Abu Abdullahasws said: ‘There is no word lighter upon the tongue than it, nor any more eloquent than ‘Glory be to Allahazwj’’. I said, ‘Would it suffice me during the Rukū and the Sajdah if I was saying in place of the Glorification, ‘There is no god except for Allahazwj, and the Praise is for Allahazwj, and Allahazwj is the Greatest?’ Heasws said: ‘Yes. All that is the Mention of Allahazwj’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘I said, ‘(The sentences) ‘The praise is for Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, and there is no god except for Allah<sup>azwj</sup>’, we understand these two. So what is the interpretation of ‘Glory be to Allah<sup>azwj</sup>’?’ He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘A sense of respect for Allah<sup>azwj</sup>. Do you not see that when the man is astounded from something, he says, ‘سُبْحَانَ اللَّهِ’ ‘Glory be to Allah<sup>azwj</sup>!’?’
en.sarwar: 5. Ali has narrated from his father from ‘Abd Allah ibn al-Mughirah from Hisham ibn al-Hakam who has said the following:

“Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘No word is lighter, easier and more eloquent for the tongue than Subhana Allah (Allah is free of all defects).’ I (the narrator) then asked, ‘Can I say Tahlil (no one deserves worship except Allah), Tahmid (it is Allah only who deserves all praise) and Takbir (Allah is great beyond description), instead of Tasbih (Allah is free of all defects)?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘Yes, all of them are speaking of Allah.’

I (the narrator) said, ‘We know the meaning of Tahmid (it is Allah only who deserves all praise) and Tahlil (no one deserves worship except Allah). What is the explanation of Tasbih (Allah is free of all defects)?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘It is to speak of the glory of Allah, consider when a man is marveled because of something says, ‘Subhana Allah (Allah is free of all defects).””
